title: Duterte’s drug war is state-sanctioned, killed over 8,000 – Truth Commission
summary: 'Preliminary, but enough to say plainly [that] the killings were state-organized. The official account cannot be accepted at face value,' says Truth Commission chairperson Raul Pangalangan

blocks.text: DRUG WAR. Relatives of war on drugs victims take part in a candle-lit vigil to commemorate the 10th anniversary of former President Rodrigo Duterte’s anti-drug campaign at the Bantayog ng Bayani in Quezon City on July 1, 2026.
'Preliminary, but enough to say plainly [that] the killings were state-organized. The official account cannot be accepted at face value,' says Truth Commission chairperson Raul Pangalangan

MANILA, Philippines – A week before former president Rodrigo Duterte’s historic trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on November 30, a local truth commission released its initial report on his war on drugs.

The Philippine Truth and Reconciliation Commission (Truth Commission) said on Monday, November 23, that the so-called drug war was systemic and inflicted by Duterte’s government on thousands of victims.

“Preliminary, but enough to say plainly [that] the killings were state-organized. The official account cannot be accepted at face value. In the cases families brought to us, no one has been held to account,” said Truth Commission chairperson and former ICC judge Raul Pangalangan.

“When killings jump in the weeks after a president tells police he will protect them if they kill, when they fall almost to nothing each time the police are pulled out of the campaign, and when they continue through Christmas and All SoulsDay, the pattern points away from chance and toward policy,” the commission said in its report.
Duterte’s campaign promise in 2016 was to eliminate illegal drugs and criminality.
After he was sworn in as the 16th president in July, he immediately launched his drug war led by the Philippine National Police (PNP) and now fellow ICC co-accused, Senator Bato dela Rosa.
On his first day as president on July 1, 2016, Duterte told the PNP that even if they killed a thousand people in line of their duty, he will protect them.

blocks.caption: Duterte to PNP: ‘Do your duty and I will die for you’

blocks.text: Launched in May, the Truth Commission seeks to provide credible documentation of the killings linked to Duterte’s drug war. It held truth-telling sessions with the victims’ families to humanize drug war victims, analyze evidence, and demand accountability and reforms. Some of the findings came from these sessions, as well as from other sources.
On Monday, the commission said there were 8,230 people killed in the drug war, based on its initial count. This number is much higher compared to the government’s count.

“The governments most cited figure, 6,252, covers only deaths in police and PDEA (Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency) operations. The 12,000 to 30,000 range cited by the ICC Prosecutor draws on several published estimates. These figures count different things; no consensus exists on the number of the dead,” the commission explained.
Apart from the initial count, the commission also released the following key findings:

items: 96.6% of the victims were men in their working and parenting years.
More than half or 56% of the killings were in Metro Manila and Central Luzon
Killings fell when police were pulled out from drug war operations.
24 of 46 exhumed victims had been shot in the head, while many killings bear the marks of execution.
People arrested during the drug war campaign remain in congested jails and prisons.

blocks.caption: Duterte’s drug war is state-sanctioned, killed over 8,000 – Truth Commission

blocks.text: The Truth Commission said its initial report will be available to everyone, including the Philippine government. Pangalangan said these findings will be shared to anyone who will find it useful, even national and international government and nongovernmental organizations.
Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida, who served as one of the reactors during the Truth Commission’s event, said they will look into the findings once transferred to the Department of Justice.

“These administrative investigations…. These are these are technically not final and definitive, right? As the pieces of evidence come along or made available, right? You adjust based on what’s…the truth and what’s available,” Vida said in a mix of Filipino and English.

Duterte has been detained in The Hague, the Netherlands, since March 2025 after he was arrested due to crimes against humanity. His case stemmed from his drug war and the killings allegedly committed by the Davao Death Squad.
On November 30, the former president will be the first Asian head of state to face a trial due to crimes against humanity before the ICC. – Rappler.com
